title: Facts, figures and trends
cando: describe numbers and trends accurately, and say what they do and don’t show

about.text: Charts and figures are everywhere at work, from team meetings to reports and the news. In this lesson you learn to describe numbers and trends accurately, to talk about what will happen next, and to say clearly what a set of figures does and does not show. At the end, you present a chart from your own work or life and answer questions about it.
goals: Describe a chart accurately: rose steadily, reached a peak, levelled off.
Say how much something changed: rose by 20%, fell to 300, just over half.
Talk about the future with this time next year and by 2030.
Read a short report with figures and write a summary that states its limits.
Present a chart in two minutes and answer questions about it.

chapters.title: A team update with charts
chapters.text:
This lesson is about numbers, and how to talk about them clearly.
First, you listen to a team update. Samir leads a customer service team, and he is showing his colleague Lena some charts.
Listen to how he describes the lines on the chart. Calls rose steadily. They reached a peak in May. Then they levelled off.
Listen, too, for the small words that say how exact a figure is: about, roughly, just over half, nearly twenty.
Notice that Lena asks good questions. What was it last year? Is there anything that worries you? You will ask questions like these in the live class.

chapters.title: Describing change, and looking ahead
chapters.text:
Next, the grammar. There are two parts.
Part one is describing change. Two small words matter a lot here. By gives the size of the change. To gives the new number. Sales rose by ten per cent. Sales rose to five hundred. You can also make a noun: a rise of ten per cent.
Part two is looking ahead. This time next year, we will be using the new system. That means it will already be happening then. By 2030, the number will have doubled. That means it will be finished before then.
Listen for these forms in the conversation, and then practise them.

chapters.title: A report with figures
chapters.text:
Then you read a short report. A company asked its staff how they travel to work, and the report gives the results.
Read it for the main idea first. Then read it again slowly. The numbers are important.
Pay special attention to the part called Limitations. Good reports say what their figures cannot show: who did not answer, what was left out, and what is only an estimate. The numbers in a report are only as good as the way they were collected.
After that, you write a summary of the report. Give the main figures, and then say clearly what its limits are.

chapters.title: Presenting a chart
chapters.text:
In the live class, you present a chart from your work or your life. It could be sales, customers, your electricity bills, your running times, or the hours you study English.
You have two minutes. Say what the chart shows, describe the main trend, and point out one interesting detail. Then say one thing the chart does not show.
After that, the others ask you questions. Try to answer with exact figures.
Prepare carefully. Check every number before the class, and practise saying the big ones out loud: four hundred and fifty, just over three thousand, seventy-five per cent.

chapters.title: The book
chapters.text:
Last, you read a longer text connected with facts and figures.
Read it once for the main idea. Then read it again and answer the questions.
When you meet a number, ask yourself: where does it come from, and what does it really show? Numbers can be exact and still tell only part of the story.

warmup.prompt: Someone shows you a chart at work. What do you look at first?
warmup.note: There is no wrong answer. Many people look at the line first, because it shows the story quickly. But the title and the numbers tell you what the line actually means.

conversation.title: The monthly update
conversation.setting: Samir leads a customer service team at an energy company. At the monthly team meeting, he shows his colleague Lena two charts on the screen.
lines: Samir
Right, let's start with the first chart. This shows the number of phone calls we received each month this year.
Lena
The line goes up quite a lot at the start.
Samir
Yes. Calls rose steadily from January to April, and they reached a peak of about four thousand in May.
Lena
That was when the new website launched, wasn't it?
Samir
Exactly. Since then, calls have declined sharply. They fell by roughly thirty per cent in June, and they've levelled off at around two and a half thousand.
Lena
And what about the online chat?
Samir
The chat figures fluctuate a lot from week to week, but the overall rate is going up. Just over half of our customers now contact us by chat.
Lena
Just over half? That's a significant change. What proportion was it last year?
Samir
About a third. So the percentage has gone up by nearly twenty points.
Lena
What about waiting times?
Samir
That's the good news. The average wait has halved, from eight minutes to four.
Lena
Impressive. Is there anything that worries you?
Samir
Only a slight rise in complaints about the chat. It's small, but we'll be watching it closely. By this time next year, we'll be answering most questions online.

questions.q: When did phone calls reach their peak?
questions.why: Calls reached a peak of about four thousand in May.

questions.q: How do just over half of the customers contact the team now?
questions.why: Samir says: Just over half of our customers now contact us by chat.

questions.q: What has happened to the average waiting time?
questions.a: It has halved, from eight minutes to four.
wrong: It has levelled off at eight minutes.
questions.why: Samir says: The average wait has halved, from eight minutes to four.

phrases.text: Calls rose steadily from January to April.
They reached a peak of about four thousand in May.
phrases.use: Saying when and where a figure was highest.

phrases.text: They've levelled off at around two and a half thousand.
phrases.use: Saying that a figure has stopped rising or falling.

phrases.text: Just over half of our customers …
phrases.use: Giving a proportion in words, not exact numbers.

phrases.text: What proportion was it last year?
phrases.use: Asking for a figure to compare with.

phrases.text: By this time next year, we'll be answering most questions online.
phrases.use: Saying what will be happening at a point in the future.

items.meaning: A picture that shows numbers, for example as a line, bars or a circle.
items.example: The chart shows our sales for the last twelve months.

items.meaning: A number, especially an official one.
items.example: The latest figures show a small rise in prices.

items.meaning: An amount out of a hundred, shown with the sign %.
items.example: What percentage of your salary goes on rent?

items.meaning: A part of a whole, compared with the whole.
items.example: A large proportion of our customers are over sixty.

items.meaning: How often something happens, or how fast it changes, over a period of time.
items.example: The unemployment rate has fallen this year.

items.meaning: The highest point or level of something.
items.example: Traffic is at its peak between eight and nine in the morning.

items.meaning: To become smaller, fewer or worse.
items.example: Sales of printed newspapers have declined for years.

items.meaning: To stop rising or falling and stay about the same.
items.example: House prices rose quickly for two years, then levelled off.

items.meaning: To go up and down often, in a way that is hard to predict.
items.example: The price of fuel fluctuates from week to week.

items.meaning: To become 50% smaller, or to make something 50% smaller.
items.example: The new machine has halved the time the job takes.

items.meaning: Slowly and regularly, without sudden jumps or stops.
items.example: Our customer numbers have grown steadily since we opened.

items.meaning: Suddenly and by a large amount.
items.example: Prices rose sharply after the storm.

items.meaning: About; not exactly.
items.example: It takes roughly an hour to get there by train.

items.meaning: Large or important enough to notice, or to matter.
items.example: There has been a significant fall in complaints.

items.meaning: Small, and not very important.
items.example: There was a slight increase in costs last month.

sound.title: thirteen or thirty?
sound.explain: When you give figures, thirteen and thirty are easy to confuse. In thirteen, fourteen and fifteen, the stress is usually at the end: thirTEEN. In thirty, forty and fifty, it is at the start: THIRty. Listen, then say each group. Then say the sentences, and make every number clear.
lines: Calls fell by thirty per cent.
The longest wait fell from forty minutes to fourteen.
Just over fifty per cent of customers use the chat.

sayIt.instructions: Say Samir's lines. Record yourself, then listen back. Are the numbers clear, and does your voice go up a little on the important figures?
lines: Calls rose steadily from January to April, and they reached a peak of about four thousand in May.
Since then, calls have declined sharply.
That's the good news. The average wait has halved, from eight minutes to four.
By this time next year, we'll be answering most questions online.

spot.instructions: Look at these sentences from the conversation. The first three describe how a figure changed. The last one looks ahead.
examples: They fell by roughly thirty per cent in June.
They've levelled off at around two and a half thousand.
The average wait has halved, from eight minutes to four.
By this time next year, we'll be answering most questions online.
spot.question: Which sentence gives the size of a change? Which gives the start and the end? Which gives the level where the change stopped? And what verb form does the last sentence use?
spot.answer: Fell by thirty per cent gives the size of the change: by. From eight minutes to four gives the start and the end: from … to. Levelled off at gives the level where it stopped. We'll be answering is will + be + -ing: something that will be happening at that time in the future.

rules.title: Describing change
rule: by = the size of the change: Sales rose by 10%. Prices fell by £20.
to = the new level: Sales rose to 500. Calls fell to 2,500.
from … to = the start and the end: The wait fell from eight minutes to four.
Verb + adverb: rose steadily, fell sharply. Adjective + noun: a steady rise, a sharp fall.
Nouns: a rise of 10% (the size), a rise in sales (the thing that changed).
rules.mistake: Not: Sales rose with 10%. Say: Sales rose by 10%.

rules.title: Looking ahead: this time next year, by 2030
rule: will be + -ing = happening at a time in the future: This time next year, I'll be working in Leeds.
will have + past participle = finished before a time: By 2030, prices will have doubled.
by + a time = at that time or before it: by Friday, by the end of the year, by 2030.
A future figure is a guess, so be careful: Sales will probably have doubled by 2030.
rules.mistake: Not: This time next year I will working in Leeds. Say: This time next year I will be working in Leeds.

practice.q: Sales rose ___ 15% last year, from 2,000 to 2,300.
practice.why: by gives the size of the change: 15%.
from … to gives the start and the end.

practice.q: There has been a sharp ___ in prices this year.
practice.why: After a sharp, you need a noun: a sharp rise.

practice.q: Prices rose ___ in the spring, and then levelled off.
practice.why: An adverb describes the verb: rose sharply.

practice.q: The report shows a rise ___ 12% in online sales.
practice.why: a rise of + the size of the change: a rise of 12%.

practice.q: This time next year, I ___ in our new office in Manchester.
practice.why: will + be + -ing: something that will be happening at that time.

practice.q: By 2030, the company ___ its energy use.
practice.why: will have + past participle: finished before 2030.

practice.q: The report needs to be finished ___ Friday at the latest.
practice.why: by + a time means at that time or before it.

practice.q: The figures go up and down every week. They ___ .
practice.why: To fluctuate is to go up and down often.

practice.q: Just ___ half of the staff replied: 52%.
practice.why: 52% is a little more than half: just over half.

yourTurn.prompt: Think of a number in your life or work that has changed: your rent, your bills, your customers, your journey to work. Write three or four sentences: how it changed, using by, to, or from … to, and what you think will be happening this time next year.
starters: Over the last … years, my … has risen by …
This time next year, I'll be …
yourTurn.model: Over the last three years, my rent has risen by roughly 25%. It went from £800 a month to just over £1,000. It rose sharply in the first year and has levelled off since then. This time next year, I'll be sharing a flat with a friend, so I'll be paying half.

text.title: Staff travel survey 2026
text.body:
PRACTICE REPORT: the company and all the figures are invented.

BRAMBLETON INSURANCE
Staff travel survey 2026: summary for managers

1. Why we did the survey
From 2027, the company plans to reduce the number of parking spaces at the Riverside office. Before we make a final decision, we wanted data on how staff actually travel to work.

2. Who took part
The survey was emailed to all 640 staff at Riverside in March. 212 people replied, so the sample represents roughly a third of the workforce. Staff on long-term leave were excluded, and so were the 45 people at our Hill Street office.

3. Main findings
· Just over half of those who replied (54%) drive to work, down from 58% in 2022 and 71% in 2019.
· The proportion who come by train or bus rose from 18% to 27%.
· Cycling has doubled since 2019, but it still accounts for only 8% of journeys.
· Working from home has had the biggest effect. We estimate that on an average day, about 35% of staff are not in the office at all.

4. The trend
Car use fell sharply between 2019 and 2022, and it has levelled off since then. The figures indicate that the fall is linked to hybrid working, but they cannot prove it: a new bus route also opened in 2021.

5. Limitations
The survey has three main limitations. First, drivers may have been more likely to reply, because the email mentioned parking. Second, the 2019 and 2022 figures come from earlier surveys with different questions, so the comparison is only approximate. Third, the data covers one month, and travel in March may not represent the whole year.

6. Next steps
This time next year, we will be running a second survey at both offices. By 2028, we will have three years of results from the same survey.

gist.q: What is the report mainly about?
gist.a: how staff travel to work, and what has changed since 2019
wrong: why the company is closing the Riverside office
how to reduce the cost of parking
gist.why: It reports a survey of how staff travel to work and compares it with 2019.

gist.a: It explains what the figures cannot show.
wrong: It says what the company will do about parking.
gist.why: Section 5 lists the limitations of the survey.

detail.q: Roughly what proportion of staff replied to the survey?
detail.why: 212 of 640 staff replied: roughly a third.

detail.q: Which group was excluded from the survey?
detail.a: the staff at the Hill Street office
detail.why: Staff on long-term leave and the 45 people at Hill Street were excluded.

detail.q: What has happened to car use since 2022?
detail.why: Car use fell sharply until 2022 and has levelled off since then.

detail.q: Why can't the report say that hybrid working caused the fall in car use?
detail.a: A new bus route also opened in 2021.
wrong: Nobody at Riverside works from home.
Too many people replied to the survey.
detail.why: The figures indicate a link, but a new bus route opened in the same period.

items.meaning: Facts and figures that are collected so that people can study them.
items.example: We need more data before we decide.

items.meaning: A set of questions that you ask a large number of people, to find out what they do or think.
items.example: According to the survey, most staff want flexible hours.

items.meaning: A small group chosen from a larger one, to learn something about the whole group.
items.example: We interviewed a sample of 200 customers.

items.meaning: The general direction in which something is changing over time.
items.example: The trend is clear: more people are shopping online.

items.meaning: A short text that gives only the main points of something longer.
items.example: Could you send me a one-page summary of the report?

items.meaning: A weak point, or something that a study or a method cannot do or show.
items.example: The main limitation of the study is its small size.

items.meaning: To calculate a number roughly, without exact information.
items.example: We estimate that the repairs will cost about £5,000.

items.meaning: To show, or suggest, that something is probably true.
items.example: Early results indicate a small fall in demand.

items.meaning: To be equal to an amount, or to be a fair example of a larger group.
items.example: Online sales now represent 40% of our business.

items.meaning: To leave someone or something out, on purpose.
items.example: These figures exclude part-time staff.

items.meaning: To form a particular part of a total.
items.example: Rent accounts for almost half of my income.

model.title: A summary that states its limits
model.body:
Summary: Brambleton staff travel survey 2026
The survey asked staff at the Riverside office how they travel to work. Just over half of those who replied (54%) drive, down from 71% in 2019, while the proportion who come by train or bus rose to 27%. Car use fell sharply until 2022 and has levelled off since then. This seems to be linked to hybrid working, although the survey cannot prove it.
However, the figures have clear limits. Only a third of staff replied, and drivers may have been more likely to answer. The Hill Street office was excluded, and the 2019 figures come from a different survey. The results are a rough guide, not an exact picture.

write.task: Find a short report, article or chart with figures: from your work, your bank, your town or the news. Or use the travel survey. Write a summary of 100–150 words. Give the main figures and the trend, then say clearly what the figures do not show.
checklist: I gave the main figures with by, to, or from … to.
I described the trend: rose steadily, levelled off, fell sharply …
I said what the figures do not show, or who was left out.
I did not claim more than the figures show.

card.title: Present a chart
card.situation: Choose a chart from your work or your life: sales, customers, bills, prices, your running times or the hours you study. You can draw it yourself. You have two minutes in the live class, and then the others will ask you questions.
card.goal: Say what the chart shows, describe the main trend with exact figures, point out one detail, and say one thing the chart does not show. Then answer questions.

phrases: As you can see, … rose steadily / fell sharply.
It reached a peak of … in …, and then levelled off.
Roughly a third / Just over half of …
One thing the chart doesn't show is …
By this time next year, I expect we'll be …
prepare.notes: Write short notes, not full sentences: what the chart shows, the main trend, the highest and lowest points, one interesting detail, one thing it does not show, and what you expect next year. Check every number before the class.

doIt.liveClass: In the live class, each learner shows their chart on the screen or on paper and presents it for two minutes. The others ask at least one question each: What happened in March? What proportion is that? Then change roles.
doIt.wehel: You are my manager at work. I am going to describe a chart to you. Listen, then ask me questions about the figures, one at a time: what the numbers were, why they changed, and what the chart does not show. After five questions, tell me if I described the changes accurately, and correct my mistakes with by, to, rose and fell.

model.title: Customers at Kwame's café
lines: Kwame
This chart shows the number of customers at my café each week, from January to June.
Mei
OK. What's the main trend?
Kwame
As you can see, numbers rose steadily, from about two hundred a week in January to just over three hundred in April.
Mei
And then there's a big jump.
Kwame
Yes. They reached a peak of four hundred and fifty in the second week of May, when the weather was warm and there was a festival in the park.
Mei
What happened after that?
Kwame
They fell sharply at the end of May, and since then they've levelled off at around three hundred and fifty.
Mei
That's still a significant rise since January. Roughly how much?
Kwame
Roughly seventy-five per cent. But one thing the chart doesn't show is how much each customer spends. In winter, people stay longer and order more.
Mei
Good point. What do you expect next year?
Kwame
By this time next year, we'll be opening on Sundays too, so I hope the numbers will have risen by another ten per cent.
compare: Did you say what the chart shows, and for what period?
Did you describe the trend with exact figures, using by, to, or from … to?
Did you say one thing the chart does not show?
Did you answer the questions with numbers, not just yes or no?

canDo: I can describe a chart accurately, with rose, fell, reached a peak and levelled off.
I can say how much something changed, using by, to and from … to.
I can talk about the future with this time next year and by + a date.
I can write a summary of a report and say what its figures do not show.
I can present a chart in two minutes and answer questions about it.

reading.before: Look at the title and any numbers or charts on the first pages. What do you think the text is about? Which numbers do you expect to be important?
reading.talk: Choose one number from the text. Where did it come from, and what does it really show? What does it not show? Write three or four sentences, or say them to Wehel.

quiz.q: Our costs rose ___ 8% last year, from £50,000 to £54,000.
quiz.why: by gives the size of the change: 8%.

quiz.q: The number of visitors fell from 900 ___ 600.
quiz.why: from … to gives the start and the end.

quiz.q: Prices went up and down all year. They ___ a lot.
quiz.why: To fluctuate is to go up and down often.

quiz.q: This time next year, we ___ the new software.
quiz.why: will + be + -ing: something that will be happening then.

quiz.q: By the end of the year, our sales ___ .
quiz.why: will have + past participle: finished before a time in the future.

quiz.q: 52% of the staff replied. That is ___ half.
quiz.why: 52% is a little more than 50%: just over half.

quiz.q: A small group chosen from a larger one, to learn about the whole group, is a ___ .
quiz.why: A sample stands for the larger group.
had + past participle: it happened before I arrived.

quiz.q: I wish I ___ that email. It caused a lot of trouble.
quiz.why: A regret about the past: wish + had + past participle.

quiz.q: The minister is said ___ her job next month.
quiz.why: Subject + is said + to + verb: is said to be leaving.

liveClass: Day 1: practise Samir and Lena's conversation in pairs. Then draw three quick line charts on the board; learners describe each one with rose, fell, reached a peak and levelled off, and give the figures with by and to.
Day 2: the task. Each learner presents a chart from their work or life for two minutes; the others ask at least one question each. Note mistakes with by and to for feedback at the end.
Day 3: talk about the book: which numbers in it matter, and what do they not show? Then two learners read their summaries aloud, and the group checks that each one states its limits.
